strengths: The paper introduces the Perception Characteristics Distance (PCD) metric to quantify the maximum distance at which a perception system reliably detects an object, addressing an important gap in static frame-level metrics for ADS/ADAS.

It presents the SensorRainFall dataset, a controlled clear-vs-rain collection with camera/radar/LiDAR and ground-truth annotations, enabling study of weather effects on detection reliability over distance.

The empirical analysis reveals heteroscedastic variance in IoU×confidence score with distance and detects more variance change points under rain for most models, providing useful insight into performance instability.
Evaluation of five SOTA detectors shows mPCD can distinguish models with similar mAP but different range reliability (e.g., Grounding DINO vs DyHead), demonstrating the metric's potential value.
weaknesses: The variance change-point test in Eq. (6) incorrectly uses f(x_τ) as the mean for all residuals in both segments, instead of f(x_i) or segment-specific means as implied by y_i = f(x_i) + ε_i; this is a technical error that undermines the proposed change-point detection.

Modeling y = IoU×confidence as a Gaussian random variable within each segment is unjustified: y is bounded in [0,1] and often zero-inflated due to missed detections; normal tail probabilities can be inaccurate and bias PCD estimates.

The dataset is very small (595 images, one red sedan target, one test track, only clear vs rainy daylight), limiting the generalizability of the metric and the empirical claims about ADS/ADAS perception in dynamic conditions.

Evaluation is restricted to camera-only object detection for a single object class; radar and LiDAR annotations are not used, and multimodal or multi-class perception is not tested, despite the dataset's multimodal claims.

The inference protocol is unclear for missed detections and false positives: no confidence threshold is applied, only the highest-confidence 'car' box is used, and it is not specified how y is computed when no detection exists, which can bias PCD upward.
There is no validation that mPCD correlates with downstream task performance or safety, and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for the model differences on the small dataset.

mPCD averages PCD over arbitrary threshold pairs (p_t, y_t) without theoretical justification or ablation; results may depend heavily on spline parameters (K, λ), significance level, and threshold ranges, which are not analyzed.

The claim that SensorRainFall is the only publicly available controlled-environment dataset is not substantiated, and the paper lacks comparison to existing controlled weather benchmarks; the promised dataset/code URLs are blank in the manuscript, hindering reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and practically important gap: standard detection metrics (mAP, IoU, F1) are static, frame-level and event-independent, and therefore cannot express the distance-dependent reliability of a perception stack that downstream ADS/ADAS decision logic actually depends on. The motivating evidence in Figure 1 (confidence fluctuating between 0.24 and 0.90 on the same visually continuous lead vehicle) makes the problem concrete and convincing.

The proposed Perception Characteristics Distance (PCD) is formulated as a principled probabilistic quantity rather than an ad-hoc threshold crossing: variance change-point detection (penalized B-splines with SIC-based sequential hypothesis testing) partitions the IoU x confidence curve into statistically distinct regimes, a Gaussian model per segment yields a mean and variance as a function of distance, and PCD is defined as the farthest distance at which P(Y > y_t) > p_t. Aggregating over threshold pairs into mPCD is a sensible analogue of AUC-style summarization, and gives the metric a defensible, distribution-aware character.

The paper provides at least one concrete demonstration that the metric carries information mAP does not: in Table 3, DyHead and Grounding DINO have comparable mAP (0.560 vs. 0.564 in clear daylight), yet Grounding DINO attains a substantially higher mPCD (92.8 m vs. 73.1 m). This is exactly the kind of range-reliability distinction the metric is designed to expose, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence in the paper.

The SensorRainFall dataset, collected on the Virginia Smart Road with paired clear-daylight and rainy-daylight (64 mm/h) captures and precise ground-truth distances, is a reasonable controlled complement to naturalistic benchmarks such as nuScenes/KITTI/BDD100K, whose uncontrolled conditions hamper exactly this kind of consistency analysis. Public release of the dataset and open-sourced evaluation code is a plus for the community.

The qualitative trends are consistent and interpretable: more variance change points under rain (Table 2, e.g., Deformable DETR going from 0 to 3), and uniformly lower PCD/mPCD in rain (Table 3, e.g., Grounding DINO 92.8 m -> 86.6 m; Deformable DETR 106.3 m -> 57.2 m). The threshold-surface analysis in Figure 6 also gives practical guidance on the range/reliability trade-off (e.g., moderate p_t, y_t ~ 0.4-0.6 giving 90-120 m in clear and 80-110 m in rain).

The paper is generally well organized: the motivation, the statistical machinery, and the experimental protocol are laid out in a readable order, and Figures 3-6 effectively visualize the intermediate quantities (change points, spline fit, PCD surface).
weaknesses: The central claim of PCD — that it identifies the maximum distance at which an object 'can be reliably detected' — is never validated against an independent notion of reliability. There is no experiment showing that detections beyond the estimated PCD are in fact wrong (or that detections within it are in fact correct), e.g., by checking ground-truth-verified miss/false-positive rates as a function of distance, or by correlating PCD with human-judged reliability. As written, PCD is a well-defined statistic whose correspondence to actual detection failure is asserted rather than demonstrated. This is the most material gap.

The metric is not ablated or compared against simpler alternatives. It is unclear how much of PCD's behavior comes from (a) the spline mean fit, (b) the change-point segmentation, or (c) the Gaussian probability model. A distance-binned mean/variance estimate, or simply the farthest distance at which the empirical IoU x confidence exceeds y_t, would be natural baselines, and the paper does not report them. Without such ablations, the elaborate statistical apparatus is not shown to be necessary.

Several modeling choices are asserted with little justification or sensitivity analysis: K = 10 B-splines and order 3, penalty lambda = 0.6 ('which suffices in our case'), and the Gaussian assumption y_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2) for a bounded quantity (IoU x confidence in [0,1]). The normality assumption is particularly questionable in the long-range regime where the variable piles up near 0 (visible in Figures 3-5), and no normality diagnostics or robustness checks are provided. The effect of these choices on PCD/mPCD is not quantified.

Cross-model comparison of a confidence-based metric is potentially confounded by confidence calibration. The evaluated detectors are heterogeneous (YOLOX, Deformable DETR, DyHead are closed-set/deterministic; Grounding DINO and GLIP are open-vocabulary models run zero-shot with the text prompt 'car'), so their confidence scores are not on a common scale. The paper reports mPCD rankings without discussing whether the Grounding DINO > DyHead mPCD gap reflects better range reliability or merely better-calibrated scores, which is exactly the alternative explanation a reviewer would want ruled out.

The dataset contribution is very narrow relative to how it is framed. SensorRainFall contains 595 images total (278 clear, 317 rainy) of a single target object (one red sedan) on a single 200 m straight test track at a single rainfall rate (64 mm/h) from a single ego vehicle. The abstract's claim that this is 'the only publicly available dataset collected in a highly controlled environment designed for perception evaluation in ADS and ADAS' is a strong and contestable statement, and the dataset cannot support generalization claims about perception stability 'in dynamic, real-world scenarios' as stated in the conclusion.

The multimodal data is collected but not used or evaluated: the paper states the dataset contains object-level annotations for camera, LiDAR, and radar, yet all experiments use only the front camera. The LiDAR/radar annotations are neither described (format, coordinate frames, calibration) nor validated, so the practical value of the multimodal portion of the dataset is unsubstantiated.

Statistical uncertainty in the reported numbers is not quantified. No confidence intervals, bootstrap estimates, or significance tests accompany the mPCD values in Table 3 or the change-point counts in Table 2, even though the per-condition sample sizes are small (hundreds of frames) and change-point counts vary by only 1-2 between conditions. Several of the paper's comparative claims (e.g., 'Deformable DETR demonstrated the greatest sensitivity to environmental shifts') rest on differences that may not be statistically distinguishable.

Annotation quality and reproducibility details are thin: ground-truth boxes were 'manually reviewed and annotated' by researchers, but no inter-annotator agreement, annotation protocol, or bounding-box tightness criterion is reported, even though IoU — and therefore PCD — depends directly on ground-truth box quality. Likewise, no random seeds, inference settings, or per-model confidence post-processing details are given beyond the general description in Section 5.1.

The framing around 'a Certain Decision Rule' is under-delivered: the title promises analysis of PCD under a specific decision rule, but the decision-rule aspect is limited to sweeping (p_t, y_t) thresholds and reporting a surface. There is no analysis of how a real downstream module (e.g., FCW/AEB logic, which the dataset was explicitly designed to emulate) would use PCD, nor any closed-loop or decision-level evaluation.

Minor issues that nonetheless affect clarity: the abstract's dataset and code URLs are redacted; Section 5.2.1's textual description of the Grounding DINO rainy segment boundaries (e.g., '[87.833, 190.611]') does not cleanly align with the four change points listed in Table 2 (81.681, 87.833, 190.611, 217.114); and Figure 4/Figure 5 panels reuse the same (a)/(b) labels for different quantities, which is confusing.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: evaluating perception robustness under adverse weather and distance-dependent reliability, moving beyond static frame-level metrics like mAP.

Introduces a new controlled dataset (SensorRainFall) collected on the Virginia Smart Road with clear/rain conditions, multi-sensor setup, and manual annotations, which could support controlled robustness studies.
Proposes a concrete PCD/mPCD evaluation pipeline combining IoU, confidence, variance change-point detection, and probabilistic thresholding, with evaluation on five SOTA detectors.
Provides empirical evidence that performance degrades in rain and that mPCD can differ from mAP across models (e.g., Grounding DINO vs. DyHead), suggesting potential value in range-aware evaluation.
Includes open-source code and dataset links (though redacted in the submission) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset is very small (595 images total, one red-sedan target, one test track, two weather conditions) and single-class, which cannot support broad claims about ADS/ADAS perception systems. No training/validation/test splits or fine-tuning are provided; models are evaluated zero-shot, limiting conclusions about model capability.

The PCD metric is heuristic and lacks rigorous decision-theoretic justification. Multiplying IoU by confidence is arbitrary, conflates confidence calibration with localization accuracy, and the 'certain decision rule' is not well-defined. Thresholding IoU×confidence is not equivalent to standard detection thresholding.

The statistical modeling is questionable: sequential frames are treated as independent, IoU×confidence values are assumed Gaussian despite being bounded in [0,1], temporal correlation is ignored, and variance change-point detection uses a small sample (~300 frames) with fixed hyperparameters (K=10, λ=0.6, α=0.05) and no sensitivity analysis or validation of detected change points.

The PCD definition assumes monotonic probability decay with distance, but the rainy-weather results show multiple variance regimes and fluctuating performance; non-monotonic cases can make the reported maximum reliable distance unreliable. No analysis of this failure mode is provided.

The evaluation is not validated against any external ground truth of reliable detection range or downstream task performance (e.g., braking, planning, collision avoidance). The claim that mPCD captures differences mAP overlooks is supported mainly by one example and may reflect confidence calibration rather than true range reliability.

Related work is incomplete: it omits adverse-weather detection datasets (e.g., ACDC, Foggy Cityscapes, Rainy Cityscapes), calibration/uncertainty literature, and distance-aware or probabilistic detection metrics, making novelty positioning weak. The claim of being the only controlled ADS/ADAS perception dataset is likely overstated.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: data collection calibration, sensor synchronization, ground-truth distance acquisition, annotation protocol/inter-annotator agreement, model inference details (NMS, handling missing detections, seeds), and statistical significance/error bars are not reported.

Experiments lack statistical rigor and breadth: no multiple runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests for mPCD comparisons; only five models are evaluated on one object class; radar/LiDAR modalities are collected but not used in the evaluation, despite being highlighted as a dataset contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: standard frame-level metrics (AP, IoU, F1) do not capture distance-dependent stochastic reliability, which matters for ADS/ADAS safety. The proposed PCD/aPCD and safety-envelope framing are practically motivated.

Introduces the SensorRainFall dataset: controlled weather/illumination conditions, multimodal sensing, manual bounding-box and segmentation annotations, and two target objects. This is a useful, if limited, resource for robustness evaluation.

Provides a reasonably broad benchmark over 10 off-the-shelf models (5 detection, 5 segmentation) and four environmental conditions, with examples where aPCD diverges from AP metrics (e.g., GLIP vs. DyHead in rainy night; Mask2Former vs. ConvNeXt-V2).

High-level method description is clear, and the paper releases dataset/evaluation code, supporting reproducibility in principle. Simulation studies for variance change-point detection assess sample size and effect size.
weaknesses: The variance change-point detection formulation appears technically inconsistent. Eq. (7) uses f(x_tau) rather than f(x_i) in the residual sums for both segments, contradicting the earlier spline mean model f(x_i). This likely biases variance estimates and change-point locations; no derivation or real-data validation is provided.

PCD/aPCD is heuristic and under-specified. The IoU×confidence product is not theoretically justified; the exact aPCD integration range/grid over p_thres and y_thres is not stated; hyperparameters (K=10, λ=0.6, α=0.05) are chosen without sensitivity analysis. The metric may favor underconfident or miscalibrated models, since confidence calibration is not addressed.

No uncertainty quantification is reported for PCD/aPCD. Differences used to rank models are sometimes <1 m (e.g., Mask2Former 23.547 vs. ConvNeXt-V2 23.448), with no confidence intervals, bootstrap, or statistical tests; this undermines claims that aPCD captures meaningful reliability differences.

The normality assumption for Y=IoU×confidence is questionable: Y is bounded in [0,1], often skewed and zero-inflated at far distances. The paper does not validate the distributional fit, so PCD probabilities near the failure tail may be unreliable.

Dataset limitations and inconsistencies reduce impact: only 1,231 images and two target objects; targets are placed one lane offset from the ego path, not in-lane, which may not reflect forward-collision/emergency-braking scenarios; rainfall rate is reported as 64 mm/h in the main text but as 20/40 mm/h in the supplement; temporal correlation across sequential frames is ignored.

Evaluation lacks key baselines and downstream validation. There is no comparison to uncertainty-aware metrics (PDQ, JIoU, oLRP) or simple distance-stratified AP baselines, and no demonstration that PCD correlates with TTC/AEB/control outcomes despite the safety motivation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the aPCD integration limits and threshold grid are not specified, change-point test details are hard to verify from the manuscript, and the controlled facility details are partially redacted/absent.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel distance-dependent reliability metric, PCD/aPCD, that explicitly models detection uncertainty and heteroscedasticity across distance, in contrast to static AP/IoU/F1 metrics.
The probabilistic formulation with adjustable thresholds p_thres and y_thres is conceptually appealing for safety-critical ADS/ADAS evaluation and enables a safety-envelope analysis.
Variance change point detection using penalized splines and SIC provides a principled way to segment distance ranges, and the included simulation studies examine sample size and effect size effects.
The SensorRainFall dataset is a useful controlled benchmark: it varies weather and illumination, provides ground-truth distances, bounding boxes, and segmentation masks, and is publicly released.
The benchmark spans 16 experiments over 5 detection and 5 segmentation models, and the results show cases where aPCD captures model differences not reflected by AP/AR/F1.
The paper is generally clear about the motivation and experimental setup, and the supplementary material provides detailed model configurations and complete benchmark tables.
The work addresses an important practical problem for autonomous driving: assessing whether perception outputs remain reliable as distance and environmental conditions change.
weaknesses: The metric relies on IoU × confidence, but confidence scores are typically uncalibrated and not comparable across model families (e.g., open-vocabulary GLIP vs closed-set detectors). Cross-model aPCD rankings may therefore reflect confidence scale rather than actual reliability; no calibration analysis is provided.

The statistical model assumes y_i = IoU × confidence is normally distributed within each distance segment, but y_i is bounded in [0,1] and often zero-inflated at far distances. This makes the normal likelihood, probability estimates, and variance change point detection potentially invalid without diagnostics or robust alternatives.

The aPCD aggregation over thresholds is not formally defined. The paper describes a 'volume under the PCD surface' over p_thres and y_thres, but omits the integration formula, threshold ranges, and discretization, making the metric difficult to reproduce and compare across papers.

The paper does not empirically compare PCD/aPCD with existing uncertainty-aware or robustness metrics such as PDQ, JIoU, LRP/oLRP, or AD, despite discussing them in related work. The claimed advantage over prior metrics is therefore not directly supported.

The evaluation protocol for standard metrics is unclear: the paper states that no confidence threshold is applied and that the highest-confidence detection is selected, yet reports AP, AR, and F1. It is not explained how AP is computed with this setup or whether the values are comparable to standard detection benchmarks.

The dataset is limited: 1,231 images, two target objects, one controlled facility, and four environmental conditions. PCD is not demonstrated on multi-class, multi-object, or crowded real-world scenes, and the radar/LiDAR modalities mentioned in the abstract are not used in the experiments.

The dataset description is inconsistent: the main text states a controlled rainfall rate of 64 mm/h, while the supplement describes two nominal rainfall intensities of 20 and 40 mm/h. This should be resolved and clarified.

Key hyperparameters (K=10, λ=0.6, α=0.05, and the threshold ranges for aPCD) are fixed without sensitivity analysis. PCD values and change point counts may depend on these choices, and no confidence intervals or error bars are reported for model rankings.

PCD evaluates only selected target detections and does not account for false positives, multiple simultaneous objects, or scene-level interactions, which are critical for safety assessment in real ADS/ADAS deployments.

The theoretical justification for the variance change point detection procedure is limited: the paper does not prove consistency of the sequential SIC-based testing under the assumed model, nor does it fully address mean-variance coupling in the observed data.

Some claims, such as SensorRainFall being the only publicly available dataset collected in a highly controlled environment for ADS/ADAS perception evaluation, are not sufficiently supported by a broader survey of existing controlled or adverse-weather datasets.
The provided dataset and code URLs are incomplete in the manuscript (e.g., Kaggle and GitHub links cut off), which limits reproducibility as reviewed.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely relevant problem in autonomous driving: evaluating distance-dependent perception reliability under dynamic (weather/illumination) conditions, which conventional static metrics (AP, IoU, F1) indeed fail to capture.

Proposes a joint IoU × confidence measure combined with a probabilistic, distance-segmented formulation (spline regression + variance change-point detection), which is a plausible and non-trivial integration of existing statistical tools.
Introduces the SensorRainFall dataset with controlled weather and illumination conditions, which—despite its size—could be a useful controlled benchmark for robustness studies.

Provides a broad benchmark: 10 state-of-the-art models across 16 experiments spanning two tasks (detection, instance segmentation), two target objects, and four environmental conditions, plus simulation studies (Figs. 8–9) to characterize the change-point detector.
Demonstrates at least one case (Example 2) where aPCD and AP-based rankings disagree, supporting the argument that distance-dependent reliability carries information not captured by AP.
weaknesses: The metric fundamentally depends on model confidence scores being well-calibrated, yet confidence calibration is known to be poor, especially for DETR-style models. Table 7 shows Deformable DETR attaining the highest aPCD (104.9) in clear daylight despite poor AP (0.511 AP50:95), which strongly suggests aPCD is partly measuring confidence-scale/calibration rather than true perception reliability—undermining the central claim.

The IoU × confidence product is an ad hoc joint measure with no principled justification; it conflates localization accuracy and confidence in a way whose meaning is unclear (e.g., high confidence + poor IoU vs. low confidence + high IoU collapse to similar values).

Degenerate results: for pedestrian instance segmentation under rainy night and rainy night with streetlights, all five models yield aPCD = 0.0 and zero change points (Tables 6, 10), so the metric yields no discriminative information in exactly the safety-critical low-visibility regimes it is meant to illuminate.

The dataset is very small (~1,231 images total, only ~230–350 per condition) and was collected at a single facility with just two target objects (a red sedan and a dummy pedestrian), severely limiting generality and statistical power.

Internal inconsistency: the main text states all rain was collected at a single controlled rate of 64 mm/h (p. 3), while the supplementary describes two nominal intensities of 20 and 40 mm/h (Supp. p. 1). This contradiction is not reconciled.

No validation that PCD/aPCD correlates with downstream task outcomes (TTC estimation, AEB/FCW triggering) is provided, even though TTC and safety are the explicit motivation; the claim that the metric 'supports safer ADS operation' is therefore unsubstantiated.

No empirical comparison against existing distance-aware or uncertainty-aware metrics (LPR/oLRP, PDQ, JIoU), which are cited but never benchmarked. The claimed novelty of PCD relative to this prior work is asserted rather than demonstrated.

No statistical significance testing of aPCD differences across models, which is essential given the very small per-condition sample sizes; ranking differences (e.g., GLIP vs. DyHead) may be within noise.

The metric remains decision-rule dependent: results hinge on arbitrary thresholds (p_thres, y_thres) and hyperparameters (K=10, λ=0.6, α=0.05). aPCD averaging over thresholds only partially mitigates this and is essentially an AUC-style summary, reducing the claimed distinctiveness.

Clarity/reproducibility issues: key details (the collection facility name and the dataset/code URLs) are redacted or missing in the manuscript, and much of the experimental setup is deferred to supplementary material, making the main paper hard to assess or reproduce.
